title: Alpha and Omega (Revelation 1:1–8)
hook: grace and peace from the one who is, who was, and who is to come

segments.voice: Yesterday, the word on Revelation's front door: apocalypse, the cloth pulled off. Your line was an unveiling. What did a loud headline reveal, once you looked underneath? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-eight.

From: John. To: the seven churches which are in Asia. Before any dragon or trumpet, Revelation reads like mail: who it's from, who it's to. Then the greeting, which is ordinary and not ordinary at all: "Grace be unto you, and peace, from him which is, and which was, and which is to come." These are real congregations, in real cities, with names we'll meet one by one. And the letter that reaches them opens by naming God in a strange order. Today we read the first eight verses, and stop at a pair of letters.

First, the order. You'd expect: who was, who is, who will be. Past, present, future. Instead John writes: who is, who was, who is to come. He starts with now. Some readers hear in it the name God gives Moses at the burning bush, I AM. Before God is a memory or a hope, God is present, here, today. Second, Jesus, in three titles. The letter sends grace "from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, and the first begotten of the dead, and the prince of the kings of the earth." A witness who told the truth, even to death. The firstborn from the dead. And a ruler over the rulers. For churches under pressure, that last title would land. Third, a sudden song. John can't finish his greeting without breaking into praise: "Unto him that loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood." Praise breaks into the middle of the mail. Fourth, the signature. Then God speaks, in the first person: "I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending, saith the Lord, which is, and which was, and which is to come, the Almighty." Alpha and omega are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet. Like saying A to Z. Everything that can be spelled, every word, every story, sits between those two letters. The claim isn't only that God was there at the start and will be there at the finish. It's that God holds the whole alphabet, including the messy middle where the seven churches were living, and where everybody lives.
screen: `IS, WAS, IS TO COME: NOW COMES FIRST.`
`A SONG: UNTO HIM THAT LOVED US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say the first and the last. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the first thing you did today, and the last thing you expect to do tonight. Hold them both, like bookends. Now let everything in between come gently into view: the conversations, the work, the worry, the small good things. If you pray, you can say the line quietly: I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending, and rest your whole day between those letters. If you don't, just let the day be held, start to finish, for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Alpha and Omega. The first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, and Revelation's name for the one who holds everything from A to Z.

Your line: the beginning and the end. This week ran from the Orthodox way through Koyama, Mbiti and Polkinghorne to Revelation's opening verses. Tonight, look back on it, beginning to end. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: The Greek letters alpha and omega appear on Christian altars, candles and vestments; in some churches the Easter candle is marked with them as a sign that Christ is the beginning and the end.

fork.setup: you're John, writing to seven churches in Asia. how do you begin?
options: with a warning of what's coming.
with grace and peace, from the one who is, and was, and is to come.

fork.reveal: he begins like a letter, with grace and peace. the dragons can wait; the first word to the churches is a greeting.

original.note: Greek: the first and last letters of the alphabet. God's signature in Revelation 1:8: the beginning and the ending.

trapdoor: what you thought: Alpha and Omega is just a grand title.
what it means: A to Z: God holds the whole alphabet, the start, the finish and the messy middle.
what a scholar hears: the order is, was, is to come, which some readers hear as an echo of I AM at the burning bush.

notes: 'Seven churches in Asia' is from Rev 1:4 (and 1:11). 'Asia' is the Roman province; not explained.
'For the first time in the book' God speaks in the first person at 1:8 — reading of the text; confirm (1:1–7 has no first-person divine speech in KJV).
Alpha and omega as the first and last Greek letters: standard; spoken and in games.
'Some readers hear ... I AM' (Exodus 3:14 LXX ὁ ὤν; Rev 1:4 ὁ ὢν) — attributed to some readers; confirm.
howItsDone: the Paschal candle marked with alpha and omega is a Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran custom; 'in some churches' kept general.
